message.content:
**Dominant Genetic Traits in Lions**

| Trait | What It Looks Like | Why it’s “Dominant” |
|-------|--------------------|---------------------|
| **Black (melanistic) coat** | A darker overall pelage—often called a *black* lion. | In most mammals, the allele for melanin production (*MC1R*) can act dominantly over lighter‑pigmented alleles. When present, even one copy will produce the dark phenotype. |
| **Male Mane Development** | Thick, long manes around the head/neck in adult males. | While hormone levels drive mane size, several loci involved in hair follicle proliferation show dominance when combined with high androgen exposure. |
| **Large Body Size / Robust Build** | Heavier body mass relative to other felids. | Genes linked to muscle fiber composition (MYH7, ACTN2) often exhibit additive effects, but certain variants have been shown to dominate in producing larger physiques. |

### Quick Takeaway  
In lions, the most straightforward example of a classic Mendelian dominant trait is the **presence of a melanistic (dark) coat**, which arises when at least one copy of the key pigment‑producing allele is inherited. Other traits such as mane length or body size involve more complex polygenic inheritance, but still display dominant tendencies under typical breeding scenarios.
